reason: The sources provide highly detailed, multi-site-supported facts about the discovery, mass, environment, ancient hyperactive state, and challenging imaging process of Sagittarius A* to support a highly engaging 45-second script.
story: At the center of our Milky Way lies Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole with the mass of four million Suns. Though it is quiet today, just 350 years ago it was a raging monster, releasing a million times more energy than it does now, an outburst we only detected as an echo reflecting off a nearby molecular gas cloud. For decades, this cosmic giant remained invisible, hidden behind thick interstellar dust. But in 2022, astronomers finally unveiled its first direct image. Capturing it was a nightmare. Because the hot gas around this black hole orbits in mere minutes, its appearance changed constantly—like trying to photograph a puppy chasing its tail. The Event Horizon Telescope's global network gathered so much data in 2017 that it couldn't be sent over the internet. Instead, scientists had to physically ship hard drives to supercomputers, taking five years to finally reveal our galaxy's lurking beast.
angle: To photograph our galaxy's terrifying central black hole, astronomers had to physically ship hard drives because there was too much data to transmit over the internet.

claims.claim: Sagittarius A* is a supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way galaxy.
Sagittarius A* was discovered in 1974.
It has a mass of approximately 4 million times that of our Sun.
In May 2022, astronomers released the first direct image of Sagittarius A*.
The image was captured using the Event Horizon Telescope, which is a global network of radio observatories.
This was the second confirmed image of a black hole, following the image of Messier 87's black hole in 2019.
The black hole itself cannot be seen because light cannot escape its immense gravity; instead, we see its dark shadow.
The dark shadow is surrounded by a glowing, ring-like structure of hot gas and dust falling into the black hole.
Sagittarius A* is located about 26,000 to 27,000 light-years away from Earth.
The actual data used to create this 2022 image of Sagittarius A* was collected in 2017.
It took five years of complex data processing and calculations to generate the final image from the 2017 data.

Imaging Sgr A* was much more difficult than M87* because Sgr A* is smaller, meaning the gas orbiting it completes an orbit in mere minutes, causing its brightness to change rapidly as it was being observed.
To capture the image, astronomers collected so much data that it could not be sent over the internet and had to be physically shipped on hard drives.
The hard drives were shipped to the MIT Haystack Observatory and the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy.
The size of the black hole's shadow matched and confirmed Einstein's theory of general relativity.
Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez won shares of the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for their discovery of this supermassive compact object at the galactic center.
About 350 years ago, Sagittarius A* was much more active, releasing a million times more energy than it does today.
This ancient outburst of energy was detected as an echo reflecting off a nearby molecular gas cloud called Sagittarius B2.
Interstellar dust and gas between Earth and the center of the galaxy prevent us from seeing Sagittarius A* in the visible spectrum.
The first image of Sgr A* was released at simultaneous press conferences around the world.

disputed: The exact mass of Sagittarius A* is estimated differently by German and American groups; a script should state it is 'about four million solar masses' to cover these minor variations.
The exact distance to Sgr A* is cited as 26,000 light-years by some sources and 27,000 light-years by others; a script should say 'about 26,000 to 27,000 light-years'.
